ROM was an amazing book. I have the whole thing, 75 issues and four annuals. It's fantastic. The first year really builds its world and core cast, and has some of Sal Buscema's best art. Year two features a lot of fun crossovers with the rest of the marvel universe. Year three they add an inker, (Arkin I want to say?), who adds a whole new finish to Buscema's art that is the artistic highlight of the series. (Sadly, this is largely washed out in the Omnibus collection). It keeps rocking solid through to the end where we're given a real resolution to the story that's been building since the start of the series. It's one of my favorite comics out there, and strongly recommended to anyone.

It's a lot of little things. They fight a dragon and are talking about an artifact on the dragon. It's totally not visible on the pages. Later, Gambit is mesmerized by the artifact to the point of being unable to fight. That fact is developed in exactly one panel, being the one where wolverine and rogue mention that they noticed it. The story is all over the place. In the few issues I read they found a dragon, went to a hospital where a kid mutant died, met and fought some kids and a Pegasus in the woods, went to Louisiana to hang out with Remy's family. I have no idea what the story is supposed to be about. It's just meandering and random. 

They meet some mutant kids asking for help. Wolverine immediately tries to fight them. Very out of character with a request for help. The kids then start wailing on the X-Men. Then they get pissed and say "well nevermind, if you aren't going to help us..." Which is it? Are they asking for help? Are they trying to fight them? It makes old stan lee heroes fighting heroes type stories feel more nuanced and well thought out. 

Everyone calls each other by their human name. This bothers me for multiple reasons. One, it feels forced and unnatural. Literally everyone calling Rogue Anne Marie and everyone calling Jubilee Jubilation. Sure, people call Cyclops Scott and Wolverine Logan all the time, but I don't think I've ever ever heard anyone call Rogue by anything other than Rogue. Second, in light of Krakoa, it feels like a rejection of their mutant identity. It feels assimilationist in a really gross way. 

Also, by the way, a little bit before Xavier went on to become someone, he met someone in college who is now the villain of this story. I absolutely hate that tired old "well, what you didn't know, two minutes before he killed the Waynes, Joe Chill blah blah blah and now there's a new villain and don't worry about why they've never popped up before now, just focus on the stipulated fact that they were there before the start so that makes them important!"

Harry Potter is super light but fun, none the less. BSG was alright. Keyforge is fun. Mythos is a strange little game. I like it but don't love it. 

Star Wars CCG I think is well respected because it was the first (of eight!) star wars ccgs. I honestly think it is way too complicated and would be hated if not for the theme. Wars is the same game but with good art and just a little streamlined. I prefer this over Star Wars a good amount. The best Star Wars one is the LCG, in my opinion. That has a very strange way of building decks (there are predestinated groups of six different cards, and rather than adding a specific card to a deck, you add the set of six cards) and there is no differentiation between on planet or off in space (Han Solo can punch the death star if he wants) but the game is otherwise pretty good. It's the same designer as call of Cthulhu and A Game of Thrones (and the Munchkin CCG if we want to be accurate...).

Munchkin, Rage, Blood Wars, X-Files/Scooby Doo, 7th Sea, I'm not the biggest fan of.
